title: Plain, consistent words for each step
statement: Name each step and concept one way everywhere, in plain words for what a reader thinks or does, with no internal jargon or stock assistant phrasing.
example: Complaints about the wording of taught steps, stems and instructions came back in 4 later review sections, more than any other class.
detail: A recurrence gauge over seven review records of the reading course, 183 classified entries with 54 reported defects, found that complaints about whether named steps, sentence stems and instructions were consistent came back in 4 later sections after the first review raised them, more than any other class (`grade3-reading/artifacts/codex-qa/experience-2026-09-14/recurrence/CLASSIFICATION-REVIEW-v3.md`, `grade3-reading/codex/qa-recurrence.json`). One of them asked for no machine-speak such as "run all four" (`grade3-reading/artifacts/feedback-aladdin-2026-08-25/REGISTER.md`). The course's checklist bans procedure jargon and coined names in what children read, and sweeps stock assistant phrasing, such as the guide narrating its own mechanism or restating what a button says, as its own class, since no validator caught it (`grade3-reading/artifacts/AlphaRead-QC-Checklist-v2-2026-09-04.md`). Use the same sentence stems throughout. Make a frame's wording match the procedure it teaches, and check that wording as a class of its own.
against: The gauge says its review sections have incomparable coverage, so the count shows how often the complaint came back in reports, not a rate (`grade3-reading/artifacts/codex-qa/experience-2026-09-14/recurrence/CLASSIFICATION-REVIEW-v3.md`). Not every repeated phrase should be uniform: the same proofread judged one family of aside phrases legitimately varied, not robotic (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0233-aug31-sweeps-prose-and-slotmap.qmd`, line 70).
